title: The Palmyrene Tax Tariff (CIS II 3913 / PAT 0259)
language_note: Bilingual: Palmyrene Aramaic and Greek. The longest lapidary Aramaic inscription known; the Aramaic and Greek versions are not exact translations of each other (the Aramaic is closer to the original 137 CE law, the Greek partially updated), which makes this a strong test case for translation-confidence scoring rather than a clean 1:1 pair.
findspot: Palmyra, Syria (discovered 1881); now in the Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg

notes: Palmyra sat astride the Roman/Parthian frontier and the Arabian caravan routes — the tariff is direct documentary evidence of Roman-era customs administration in a non-Roman-language legal text. Original text needs a proper transcription pass before ingestion; currently only a summary is captured. What the tariff regulates: customs duties on goods entering and leaving Palmyra and on local trades, rather than long-distance caravan tolls specifically; J.F. Healey, Aramaic Inscriptions and Documents of the Roman Period (2009) and Shifman/Healey, The Palmyrene Tax Tariff (Oxford, 2014). John Matthews describes it as 'one of the most important single items of evidence for the economic life of any part of the Roman Empire.' This is editorial and secondary-literature material, kept here so it is not citable as source evidence.
